candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.17 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The Risen Christ's words to Mary Magdalene — 'Touch me not (mē mou haptou); for I am not yet ascended to my Father' — Cyril treats with care. The 'touch me not' Cyril reads not as ritual-purity concern (the resurrection-flesh is not unclean) but as redirecting Mary's grasping affection: the post-resurrection relationship will be different in mode, mediated through the ascension and the Spirit's coming. 'I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God' Cyril reads with careful Trinitarian precision: the distinction (MY Father / YOUR Father) preserves the Son's unique-by-nature sonship as distinct from the believers' adoptive-by-grace sonship. The verse establishes the theological basis for the Tewahedo doctrine of adoptive theosis.

candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'And when He had said this, He breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost' Cyril treats as a Trinitarian-pneumatological text of extraordinary density. The breathing (enephysēsen — the same verb as in Gen 2:7 LXX, where God breathes life into Adam) Cyril reads as the deliberate new-creation parallel: the Risen Christ inaugurates the eschatological new creation by breathing the Spirit into the new humanity. The 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost' (labete Pneuma Hagion) Cyril carefully distinguishes from Pentecost: this is the Spirit-gift FOR the apostolic commission (immediately followed by 'Whose soever sins ye remit'), Pentecost is the Spirit-gift for universal indwelling. Both are real; both are sourced in Christ. The Tewahedo holy-orders prayer at episcopal consecration echoes this verse explicitly.

candidates.draft_body:
Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.26 (c. 350 AD)

'And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God' — Athanasius marks ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou (the dual-vocative with definite articles) as the unambiguous post-resurrection divinity-confession. The grammar excludes every Arian-subordinationist reading: Thomas does NOT say 'a lord and a god' (indefinite, which a creature might receive) but 'THE Lord and THE God' (definite, the singular kyrios who is THE theos). Christ accepts the confession with a beatitude (Jn 20:29 makarioi hoi mē idontes — 'blessed are they that have not seen and yet have believed') — divine-acceptance of divine-worship that would be idolatry-by-Christ if he were a creature. The Tewahedo Easter (Fāsika) liturgical-acclamation cites Jn 20:28 at the second post-resurrection Sunday (Mansǝʿu — 'Risen-One') as the Thomine-confession-of-faith.
